title: Number of Sets of K Non-Overlapping Line Segments
statement:
There are `n` points on a number line, at `x = 0, 1, ..., n - 1`. Count the ways to place exactly `k` line segments whose endpoints are two different points from this set (so every segment spans at least two points). Segments must not overlap: two of them may touch at a common endpoint, but they may not share any stretch of length. The segments do not need to cover all points. Two placements are different when their sets of segments differ.

Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Between the `n` points there are `n - 1` unit gaps. A segment is simply a run of consecutive gaps, and "non-overlapping" means no gap is used by two segments. Two segments that share an endpoint are two runs that sit right next to each other. So scan the gaps from left to right: each gap is either left empty, added to the segment that the previous gap belongs to, or used to open a brand-new segment. All that matters at each moment is how many segments have been opened and whether the last gap was covered. (Enumerating every set of segments works for tiny `n` but explodes quickly; the count also equals the binomial `C(n + k - 1, 2k)`.)

## Approach

1. `free[j]` counts placements so far with `j` segments where the last gap is empty; `inside[j]` counts those where the last gap belongs to segment `j`. Before any gap only `free[0] = 1`.
2. For each gap, build `nextFree` and `nextInside`:
   - leaving the gap empty: `nextFree[j] = free[j] + inside[j]`;
   - extending the current segment: `nextInside[j]` starts as `inside[j]`;
   - opening segment `j` here (after an empty gap or right where the previous segment ended): add `free[j - 1] + inside[j - 1]`.
3. Swap in the new arrays and continue.
4. After the last gap, the answer is `free[k] + inside[k]`, all modulo `10^9 + 7`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 4` gives 3 gaps, `k = 2`. Start: `free = [1, 0, 0]`, `inside = [0, 0, 0]`.

- Gap 0: `free = [1, 0, 0]`, `inside = [0, 1, 0]`.
- Gap 1: `free = [1, 1, 0]`, `inside = [0, 2, 1]`.
- Gap 2: `free = [1, 3, 1]`, `inside = [0, 3, 4]`.

The answer is `free[2] + inside[2] = 1 + 4 = 5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · k): each of the `n - 1` gaps updates `k + 1` counts.
- Space: O(k): only the current and next rows are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Opening a new segment is allowed right after a covered gap; that is exactly the shared-endpoint case, so add `inside[j - 1]` too.
- Extending is only possible from `inside[j]`, never from `free[j]`, or two separate runs would merge into one segment.
- Reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` on every update; the true counts grow far beyond 2^53.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `free[j]` | ways with `j` segments and the last gap empty |
| `inside[j]` | ways with `j` segments and the last gap inside segment `j` |
| `edge` | index of the gap being decided (between points `edge` and `edge + 1`) |
| `j` | number of segments opened so far |
| `nextFree`, `nextInside` | the counts after deciding the current gap |

narration.3: free[j]: ways with j segments where the last gap is not covered.
narration.4: inside[j]: ways with j segments where the last gap belongs to segment j.
narration.5: Before any gap there is exactly one way: no segments at all.
narration.7: Decide the n - 1 gaps between neighbouring points one at a time.
narration.10: Update every possible number of segments j.
narration.11: Leave this gap empty: it does not matter whether the previous gap was covered.
narration.12: Extend the segment that already covers the previous gap; the count of segments stays j.
narration.13: Opening a new segment needs at least one segment in the count.
narration.14: Start segment j on this gap, either after an empty gap or exactly where the previous segment ended.
narration.17: The new counts become the current ones for the next gap.
narration.20: After the last gap, count every way that used exactly k segments.
